title: ATM schema in PostgreSQL
idea: The ATM schema maps the Java model to tables so PostgreSQL enforces money rules: no negative balance, one row per ATM request, one locked account.

analogy.text: A bank ledger kept in one locked drawer. A clerk takes the key, checks the balance, writes the line, then hands the key on.
analogy.breaks: The row lock covers one account, not the whole ledger.

points: A CHECK on `balance_minor` refuses any overdraw the code forgot to stop.
A UNIQUE pair of `atm_id` and `request_id` makes a retry find its first row.
A partial index on account and time serves the daily-limit sum query.
Withdraw locks the account row `FOR UPDATE`, then checks, debits and records.

items.label: BEGIN
items.text: One transaction holds every read and write of this withdrawal.

items.label: Lock account
items.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the account row. Another ATM for it waits.

items.label: Replay check
items.text: Look up the request id. If found, return its stored result.

items.label: Rules
items.text: Compare the balance, then today's total plus this amount against the daily limit.

items.label: Write
items.text: Debit the balance and insert a PENDING row, or insert a DECLINED row only.

items.label: COMMIT
items.text: The lock is released. The waiting ATM now reads the new balance.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The full schema on a real PostgreSQL. Each bad write is refused by a named constraint, shown by its error code.

walk.text: `account` keeps money as BIGINT paise, and the balance can never drop below zero.
`card` stores a token and a PIN hash, never the card number or PIN.
One cassette row per ATM and note value; counts cannot go negative.
Status is TEXT with a CHECK; one row per ATM request id.
The partial index holds only rows that count toward the daily limit.
Five writes: one ok, then a duplicate, an overdraw, too few notes and a bad foreign key.
Today's total uses a half-open range on `created_at`, which the index serves.

code.title: The withdrawal transaction
code.caption: Two ATMs withdraw from one account at once, then a retry, a reversal and the daily limit.

walk.text: Lock the account row first, so every withdrawal for it runs one at a time.
Inside the lock, a known request id is a replay: return the stored status.
Sum today's spending, then decline for funds or limit, or debit.
Record the row either way and commit, which releases the lock.
Reverse flips PENDING to REVERSED and credits back. A second call changes no row.
Run two withdrawals in parallel. The lock, not timing, decides the result.
Replay the winner, reverse it twice, then hit the daily limit.

pitfalls: Check the request id after taking the lock; otherwise a parallel retry fails with 23505.
Pass day boundaries as parameters; `date_trunc` depends on the session time zone.
Never store card numbers or PINs; store a token and a salted PIN hash.

quiz.q: What does withdraw.mjs print for the two parallel ATMs?
quiz.why: The second transaction waits on the row lock. It then reads balance 20000, which is below 80000, so it declines for funds.

takeaway: Lock the account row, then check, debit and record in one transaction.

starters: Why lock the account row instead of using a version column?
Should DECLINED attempts be stored in the same table?
How would I keep a full ledger of debits and credits?
